summary:
TERRANALOG is a web app, live at terraanalog.netlify.app, that matches Earth environments to the places NASA plans to use for permanent Moon bases and Mars exploration. You pick one of 7 targets (5 on the Moon and 2 on Mars), and the app ranks 12 Earth sites, like the Atacama Desert in Chile and Devon Island in Canada, by how closely they match.

Each place is scored on 8 things: temperature, terrain, geology, water and ice, underground space, dust, signs of life and rover mobility. You can use sliders to change what matters most, and the ranking updates right away. The temperature score uses live NASA POWER climate data. You can also click anywhere on the map to see how well that spot matches your chosen target.

The app has four sections: a Discovery Lab for ranking, a Global Map, a Moon & Mars comparison page and a Scientific Brief. It also says clearly which scores are measured and which are estimated, and it includes a possible analog site in Balochistan, Pakistan, the Kharan-Chagai Desert.
details:
What does it do?

TERRANALOG helps you find places on Earth that are similar to the places NASA wants to build Moon bases and explore on Mars. You pick a target, like Shackleton Crater on the Moon or Jezero Crater on Mars, and the app gives you a ranked list of 12 Earth sites, like the Atacama Desert in Chile and Devon Island in Canada. Each site gets a match percentage, so you can see which one is closest to your target.

For every site, the app also tells you what it is useful for, like testing lava tubes, ice or rover driving. It also tells you where the site is not like the Moon or Mars. You can look at a map, compare sites on a chart and download the results. In short, it helps a team decide where on Earth to test equipment before sending it to space. The app is live on Netlify at https://terraanalog.netlify.app, so anyone can open it in a web browser.

How does it work?

Every Earth site and every Moon or Mars target is described with the same 8 scores: temperature extremes, terrain, geology, water and ice, underground space, dust, signs of life and how easy it is for a rover to move. The app compares these scores and gives each site a match percentage. You can also move sliders to decide what matters most. If you care more about water than terrain, the ranking changes right away.

The temperature score comes from live climate data from NASA POWER. You can also click anywhere on the map, and the app pulls the climate for that spot and tells you if it is a strong, moderate or weak match for your target. The terrain score uses a formula with slopes we estimated, and the other six scores come from published studies.

What benefits does it have?

It saves time. Instead of reading many papers to find a good test site, you can compare sites in one place. It also shows where each Earth site fails to match, because Earth can’t copy low gravity, a vacuum or space radiation. It works for anyone, even without a paid map key, because it switches to a free map by itself. Because we deployed it on Netlify, there is nothing to install. You just open the link.

What is the intended impact of the project?

We want to make choosing analog sites easier and more open for students, researchers and mission planners. Testing rovers and equipment on Earth first is cheaper and safer than testing in space. We also wanted to bring attention to our own region, so we added the Kharan-Chagai Desert in Balochistan, Pakistan, as a possible analog site that still needs to be checked by scientists. Our score is a starting point for exploring, not a final scientific result.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Coding languages: TypeScript, HTML and CSS

Frameworks: React, Vite and Tailwind CSS

Maps: Leaflet with Esri map tiles, and Google Maps as an optional extra

Data: NASA POWER API for live climate data

Charts: a radar chart built with SVG

Other services: BigDataCloud, to find the country name for a point on the map

Tools: Node.js, npm and GitHub, to build and share the code

Hosting: Netlify, to deploy the app online

Hardware: no special hardware, because it runs in a normal web browser

AI tools: used to help with parts of the coding, the images and the writing, while our team decided the idea, the scope and the final work

How is your project creative?

Most analog lists are fixed. Ours is interactive, so you can change the priorities and watch the answer change. The click-anywhere map lets people test any place on Earth. We also put the Moon and Mars together in one tool, and we added a local site from Pakistan that most projects wouldn’t think of. We were also honest in the app about what is measured and what is estimated.

What factors did your team consider?

First, honesty about our data. Only the temperature score uses live NASA data. The terrain score uses a formula with slopes we estimated, and the other six scores come from published studies. We say this clearly in the app. Second, the limits of Earth: gravity, atmosphere and radiation can’t be copied here. Third, uncertainty, like the Kharan-Chagai site and the possible cave under Mare Tranquillitatis. We also thought about making the tool free to use, easy to understand and open about its sources. In the future we want to replace our estimates with real satellite data and search the whole Earth for new analog sites.
